parole.significato: forms nouns representing the property corresponding to an adjective; -ity
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -tātem, from Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts.
Borrowed from Latin -itātem.
Inherited from Old Catalan aygua~ayga, from Latin aqua, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂. First attested in 1169. Compare Occitan aiga, French eau, Spanish agua.
Borrowed from Latin anteriōrem.
Inherited from Old Catalan aradre, from Latin arātrum (compare Occitan araire, Spanish arado), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂érh₃trom.
Inherited from Latin arcus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erkʷo-.
Inherited from Latin arca.
Borrowed from Latin avārus.
Inherited from Latin basium, from Proto-Indo-European *bu. Compare Occitan bais, Spanish beso, Italian bacio.
Inherited from Latin blandus.
Borrowed from Latin bēstia (“beast”). Compare French bête, Sicilian vèstia.
Inherited from Latin campus (compare Occitan camp, French champ, Spanish campo), from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂emp- (“to bend, curve”).
Borrowed from Latin caulis. Doublet of col.
Inherited from Latin collum. Compare Occitan còl, French cou, and Sicilian coḍḍu.
Inherited from Latin corvus, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorh₂wós. First attested in the 14th century.
Borrowed from Latin creāre. Doublet of criar (“to raise”).
Inherited from Latin cremāre, from Proto-Indo-European *ker (“to burn”). Compare Occitan cremar, Spanish quemar.
Borrowed from Latin creatūra.

parole.significato: crust (any hard surface layer; surface layer of most breads and pastries)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin crusta (“bark, crust, shell”) (compare Occitan crosta, French croûte, Spanish costra), from Proto-Indo-European *krustós (“hardened”), from *krews- (“to form a crust, begin to freeze”). The /ɔ/ is unexpected and perhaps due to influence from other words with similar meanings.
Inherited from Latin cūlus.
Inherited from Latin cūra, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeys- (“to heed”).
Inherited from Latin carcer. Compare Spanish cárcel.
Learned borrowing from Latin cumulus.
Borrowed from Latin dēnsus.

parole.significato: indicates the negation of a verb; dis-, un-
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin dis-, from Proto-Indo-European *dwís. Doublet of dis-, which was borrowed.
Inherited from Latin decem, from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥.

parole.significato: axle (pin or spindle on which a wheel revolves)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin axem (compare Occitan ais, French ais, Spanish eje), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs- (“axis”).
Inherited from Latin mē, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁mé.
Inherited from Latin inter, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁enter (“between”). First attested in the 12th century.
Inherited from Latin ignōrāre (“to ignore”). Doublet of borrowed ignorar.
Inherited from Latin ērūca, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰer(s)-uk-eh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰers- (“to bristle”). Compare Occitan eruga, Sardinian ruga.
Inherited from Latin scūtum, from Proto-Indo-European *skei- (“to cut, split”). Compare Occitan escut, French écu, Spanish escudo.

parole.significato: to scatter, to strew, to spread
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin spargere (“scatter”), with normal change of conjugation to -ir; from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pregʰ- (“to scatter, to jerk”).
Inherited from Latin spissus, from Proto-Indo-European *spidtos. Compare Occitan espés, French épais, Spanish espeso.
Borrowed from Latin stimulāre.
Borrowed from Latin stimulus.
From Latin exsequor (“to pursue”), from ex- (“out”) + sequor (“to follow”), Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to follow”).
Borrowed from Latin exsūdāre (“to sweat out”), from ex- with sūdāre (“to sweat”), from sūdōris (“of sweat”), from Proto-Indo-European *swoyd- or *sweyd-.
Inherited from Latin falcem (compare Occitan fauç or hauç, French faux, Spanish hoz) from Proto-Indo-European *dʰelk-, *dʰelg- (“a cutting tool”).
Inherited from Latin famēs (“hunger”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰH- (“to disappear”). Compare Occitan fam or Occitan hami.
Borrowed from Latin fama, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂-mā-, from *bʰeh₂- (“to speak”).
Inherited from Latin fidem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ-. First attested in the 12th century. Compare Occitan fe.

Inherited from Old Catalan fe, from Latin fēnum, monophthongized variant of faenum, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)-no-, from *dʰeh₁(y)-. The modern form fenc, which appears to have been taken from a northeastern dialect, has the advantage of distinguishing the word from fe (“faith”). Compare Occ
Inherited from Latin ferus (compare Occitan fèr, French fier, Spanish fiero), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰwer-.
Borrowed from Latin fibra.
Inherited from Latin forās (“outside”) (compare Occitan fòra, French hors, Spanish fuera), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwer- (“door; gate”).
Inherited from Latin formīca (compare Occitan formiga, French fourmi, Spanish hormiga), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *morwi-.

parole.significato: dark (having an absolute or relative lack of light)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin fuscus. Compare Occitan fosc, Dalmatian fosc, Spanish hosco, Portuguese fosco, fusco or Italian fosco, Old French fusque.
Inherited from Latin frīgere, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer-.
Inherited from Latin fraxinus (“ash tree”) (compare Occitan fraisse, French frêne, Spanish fresno), from *bʰr̥Hǵ-s-inos, adjective of Proto-Indo-European *bʰerHǵos (“birch”).
Inherited from Latin frontem, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰron-t-, from *bʰren- (“project”). Compare Occitan front, French front, Spanish frente.
Inherited from Latin gallus, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gelH-.
Inherited from Old Catalan gel, from Latin gelū, from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”).
Inherited from Old Catalan geniva, from Latin gingīva (compare Occitan gengiva, French gencive, Spanish encía), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵyewh₁-.
Inherited from Old Catalan gent, from Latin gentem, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁tis.
Inherited from Old Catalan gola, from Latin gula, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷel- (“throat”).

parole.significato: grain, the seed of various grass crops
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin grānum (compare French grain, Occitan gran, Spanish grano), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm. Cognate with Portuguese grão, Occitan and Galician gran, and Spanish grano.
Inherited from Old Catalan gran, grant, grand, from Latin grandis, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ghrewə- (“to fell, put down, fall in”).
Inherited from Latin gruem (“crane”), from *gr̥h₂ú-, from Proto-Indo-European *gerh₂- (“to cry hoarsely”).
Inherited from Old Catalan erba, from Latin herba, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow, become green”).
Learned borrowing from Latin intrā (“within”).
Learned borrowing from Latin laxus.
Borrowed from Latin laesus.
Inherited from Latin lacus (“lake”), from Proto-Indo-European *lókus (“lake, pool”).
Inherited from Old Catalan lavar, from Latin lavāre, from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃-.
Inherited from Old Catalan lenya, from Latin ligna, plural of lignum (compare Occitan lenha, Spanish leña, Italian legna), from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-no- (“that which is collected”), from *leǵ-.
Inherited from Old Catalan ligar, from Latin ligāre, from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵ- (“to bind”).
Borrowed from Latin līma.

Inherited from Latin līnea (“thread, line”), from līnum (“flax”), from Proto-Indo-European *līno- (“flax”). Doublet of línia. Cognate with Spanish and Galician liña, Spanish línea, and Portuguese linha.
Inherited from Old Catalan lum, from Latin lūmen (compare Spanish lumbre), from Proto-Indo-European *léwksmn̥, derived from the root *lewk- (“bright”). Compare Occitan lum, Spanish lumbre.
Inherited from Latin lācrima (compare Occitan lagrema, French larme, Spanish lágrima), from Old Latin lacruma, dacrima, dacruma, from Proto-Indo-European *dáḱru-.

parole.significato: line (path through two or more points)
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin līnea (“thread, line”), from līnum (“flax”), from Proto-Indo-European *līno- (“flax”). Doublet of the inherited llinya. Cognate with Spanish and Galician liña, Spanish línea, and Portuguese linha.
Inherited from Old Catalan madur, from Latin mātūrus (compare Occitan madur, French mûr, Spanish maduro), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂- (“to ripen, mature”).
Inherited from Old Catalan margen, from Latin marginem (compare Occitan marge, French marge, Portuguese margem), from Proto-Indo-European *mórǵs.
Inherited from Old Catalan ment, from Latin mentem (“mind”), from Proto-Indo-European *méntis (“thought”).
Inherited from Old Catalan mes, from Latin mēnsem (“month”), from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon, month”). Compare Occitan mes, French mois, Spanish mes.
Inherited from Latin mŭccus, an alternative form of mūcus, from Proto-Indo-European *mew-k- (“slimy, slippery”).

Inherited from Old Catalan moyll, from Latin mollem, from earlier *molduis, from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥dus (“soft, weak”), from *(s)meld- (“soft, weak, tender”). Compare Occitan mòl, French mou, Spanish muelle.
Learned borrowing from Latin morbus.
Inherited from Old Catalan mosca, from Latin musca, from Proto-Indo-European *mus-.
Inherited from Old Catalan mur, from Latin mūrus, from Old Latin *moerus, *moiros, from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to strengthen”).
Inherited from Old Catalan mut, from Latin mūtus, of Proto-Indo-European origin.
Inherited from Old Catalan nas, from Latin nāsus, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s.
Inherited from Old Catalan nau, from Latin nāvem, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us. Cognate with English nave, navigate, and navy.
Inherited from Old Catalan neula, from Latin nebula, from Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos (“cloud”). Compare Occitan nèbla, Portuguese névoa, Spanish niebla.

parole.significato: name (word that indicates a particular person, place, or thing)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan nom, from Latin nōmen, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥.
Inherited from Latin nōnāgintā (“ninety”), from earlier *nūnāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥(d)ḱomt (“nine tens”). Compare Occitan nonanta, French nonante; cf. also Spanish noventa.
Inherited from Latin novem (“nine”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥. Compare Occitan nòu.
Inherited from Latin nūdus, from Proto-Indo-European *nogʷós.

Inherited from Latin audīre, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew-is-d-, a compound of Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewis (“clearly, manifestly”) (from the root *h₂ew- (“to see, perceive”)) and *dʰh₁-ye/o- (“to render”). Doublet with audir.
Inherited from Latin olōrem, a non-Classical counterpart to Latin odōrem, likely influenced by olēre (“to smell”), both ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed- (“to smell, stink”).
Inherited from Old Catalan ombra, from Latin umbra, probably from Old Latin *omra, possibly from a Proto-Indo-European *h₂mr-u-, *h₂mrup-.
Inherited from Latin unda, from Proto-Indo-European *unt-. Doublet of onda, a semi-learned form.
Inherited from Old Catalan pa (attested at least once as pan), from Latin pānis, possibly derived from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to graze, feed”).
Inherited from Old Catalan palla, from Latin palea, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“flour, dust”). Compare Occitan palha, French paille, Italian paglia, Sicilian pagghia, Spanish paja.
Inherited from Latin palma, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₂meh₂.

parole.significato: to stop (a person, an animal, a machine) from continuing movement or action
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan parar, from Latin parāre, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“produce, procure, bring forward, bring forth”). First attested in the 13th century.
Inherited from Old Catalan pau, from Latin pācem, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ-. Compare Occitan patz, French paix, Spanish paz.
Inherited from Latin piscem, from Proto-Indo-European *peysk-.

parole.significato: pine; evergreen tree of the genus Pinus
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan pin, from Latin pīnus, ultimately from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *poi- (“sap, juice”).
Inherited from Latin peiōrem, from Proto-Indo-European *ped-yōs (“to the ground, downward”). First attested in the 14th century.
Inherited from Old Catalan plan, from Latin plānus, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂-. Compare Occitan plan, French plain, Spanish llano.
Inherited from Latin plicāre, from Proto-Indo-European *pleḱ- (“plait, weave”).
Inherited from Old Catalan pobre, from Latin pauper, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w- (“few, small”). Compare Occitan paure~paubre, French pauvre, Spanish pobre.
Inherited from Old Catalan porta, from Latin porta, from the Proto-Indo-European root *per- (“to pass through”).
Inherited from Old Catalan portar, from Latin portāre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“go, traverse”).
Inherited from Old Catalan prendre, from Latin prēndere, from older prehendere, from prae- (“before”) + hendere (“take, seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed-.
Borrowed from Latin proximus. First attested in 1599.
Borrowed from Latin pulmōnem, from Proto-Indo-European *pléwmō. First attested in the 14th century.
Inherited from Old Catalan pus, from Latin plūs, from Old Latin *plous, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁-, *pelh₁u- (“many”). Compare Occitan pus, French plus.
Learned borrowing from Latin pāgina.
Inherited from Latin passer (“sparrow”).
Inherited from Latin pilus, from Proto-Indo-European *pil-.
Inherited from Latin quattuor (“four”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres. Compare Occitan quatre, French quatre, and Spanish cuatro.
Inherited from Latin quid, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷid, compare *kʷís.
Borrowed from Latin rēctus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵtós (“straightened, right”).
Inherited from Old Catalan rei, reig, from Latin rēgem, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs (“ruler”).
Inherited from Old Catalan riba, from Latin rīpa, from Proto-Indo-European *rey- (“to tear, cut”).
Borrowed from Latin ruptūra.

parole.significato: ruin (the remains of a destroyed or dilapidated construction)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ruīna.
From Old Catalan sa~san, from Latin sānus, from Proto-Indo-European *swā-n- (“healthy; whole; active; vigorous”).
Inherited from Old Catalan salut, from Latin salūtem, related to salvus (“safe”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- (“whole, completed”).
Inherited from Latin salix (compare Spanish sauce, Italian salce), from Proto-Indo-European *sl̥H-ik- (“willow”).
Inherited from Old Catalan sech, from Latin siccus (“dry”), from Proto-Indo-European *seyk-.

Inherited from Old Catalan sexanta, from Latin sexāgintā (“sixty”), from Proto-Indo-European *sweḱsḱomt, from earlier *swéḱs-dḱomt (“six-ten”). Compare Occitan seissanta, French soixante, Spanish sesenta.
Inherited from Old Catalan selva, from Latin silva, from Proto-Indo-European *sel-, *swel- (“beam, board, frame, threshold”). Compare Occitan selva, Spanish selva.
Borrowed from Latin sēmi-.
Inherited from Old Catalan seny, from Latin signum (“signal”), of Proto-Indo-European origin. The meaning of "bell" is attested from the 6th century onwards. Doublet of the borrowing signe.
Inherited from Old Catalan serp, from Latin serpēns, derived from serpō (“crawl, creep”), from Proto-Indo-European *serp-.
Inherited from Latin septem (“seven”), from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥. Cognates include Occitan sèt.
Inherited from Latin sitis, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰgʷʰítis.
Inherited from Latin septuāgintā (“seventy”), from *septmāginta, from Proto-Indo-European *septm̥̄ḱomt, from earlier *septḿ̥-dḱomt (“seven-ten”).
Inherited from Old Catalan sèu, from Latin sēbum (“tallow, grease; suet”), from Proto-Indo-European *seyb- (“to pour out”).
Inherited from Latin sex, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs.
Inherited from Old Catalan sobre, from Latin super (“above”), from *eks-uper, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰs (“out of”) (Latin ex) and *uperi (“above”), from *upo. Doublet of the borrowed súper.

Inherited from Old Catalan sofre, from Latin sulfur, from Proto-Indo-European *swelplos, from the root *swel- (“to burn, smoulder”). Doublet of the borrowed form sulfur. Compare Occitan solpre, French soufre, Spanish azufre.
Inherited from Old Catalan sol, from Latin sōlem (“sun”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥.
Inherited from Latin sulcus, from Proto-Indo-European *solk-o- (“furrow”), *selk- (“to pull, drag”).
Borrowed from Latin somnium. Compare the inherited Old Catalan suny. See also the related son (“sleep”).
Inherited from Old Catalan son, from Latin somnus, from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos. Feminine noun by analogy with fam (“hunger”) and set (“thirst”).
Inherited from Old Catalan sord, from Latin surdus, from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“ringing, whistling”).
Inherited from Old Catalan suar, from Latin sūdāre, a verb based ultimately on Proto-Indo-European *sweyd-. Compare Occitan susar, suar, sudar; French suer; Spanish sudar.

Inherited from Old Catalan tendre, from older tenre (with epenthesis), from Latin tener (“soft, tender”), from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch, draw”). Compare Occitan tèndre, French tendre, Spanish tierno.
Inherited from Old Catalan tenyir~tènyer~tínyer, from Latin tingere, from Proto-Indo-European *teng- (“to soak, dip”). Compare Occitan ténher, French teindre, Spanish teñir.
Inherited from Old Catalan terme, inherited from Latin terminus, from Proto-Indo-European *ter-.

parole.significato: third (one of three equal parts of a whole)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin tertius (“third”), from trēs (“three”), from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes.
Inherited from Old Catalan tord (also spelled tort), from Latin turdus (“thrush”), from Proto-Indo-European *trosdos. Compare Occitan tord (and tordre), Spanish tordo.
Inherited from Latin trāns (“across, beyond”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₂- (“through, throughout, over”). Doublet of tras- and trans-.
Inherited from Latin trāns (“across, beyond”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₂- (“through, throughout, over”). Doublet of tra- and trans-.
Inherited from Old Catalan trenta, from Latin trigintā, from Proto-Indo-European *tri(d)ḱomt (“thirty”).
Inherited from Latin truncus.
Inherited from Old Catalan ungla, from Latin ungula, diminutive of unguis (“claw, hoof”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃negʰ-.
Borrowed from Latin unguentum.
Inherited from Latin vacca.
Borrowed from Latin vēlōcem.
Inherited from Old Catalan vena, from Latin vēna, of uncertain Proto-Indo-European origin.
Borrowed from Latin vetō.

parole.significato: to veto (to use a veto against)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vetāre.
Inherited from Latin vicem.
Derived from Latin vice.
Inherited from Latin ōra. Compare Spanish orilla.
Inherited from Latin octō (“eight”), from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw.
Inherited from Old Catalan vuytanta~huytanta, from Latin octāgintā, variant of octōgintā (“eighty”), from Proto-Indo-European *oktōḱomt, from earlier *oḱto(w)-dḱomt (“eight-ten”).
Borrowed from Latin victima.
Alteration of Old Catalan ànet, from Latin anătem, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énh₂t- (“duck”); probably due to a common pronunciation of the plural ànets as ànecs.
Borrowed from Latin orbita.
Borrowed from Latin uterus.
